lesson.subtitle: Lesson 9 -- Reporting Back to Tokyo
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Julius Cesar do Nascimento | Lesson 9 -- Reporting Back to Tokyo
lesson.grammar_point: reported speech: backshift, reported questions (asked if / whether / wh-), reporting verbs (said, told, suggested, promised, warned)

listenings.text: I manage software projects in Bangalore, and my clients are in London, Chicago and Tokyo. After a long client meeting, my director never wants the full story. He wants three lines. What did they say, what do they want, and what do I need from him. Last week, for example, the meeting took two hours. My report was three sentences. The client said that they were happy with the quality, but worried about the delivery dates. They asked whether we could add two more people to the team. And I need my director to approve the budget by Friday. That's it. One thing I never do is repeat every word that was said. My director doesn't have time for that, and honestly, nobody does.

A few years ago, I learned how dangerous a bad report can be. One of our sales managers met a big customer in Rotterdam. The customer said that they might need more parts next year. Might, not will. But the report that went to headquarters said that the customer had promised to double the order. Headquarters believed it, and they started to plan a new production line. Three months later, the customer ordered exactly the same quantity as before. Nobody had lied. One person had chosen the wrong verb. Since then, I have one rule. After every important meeting, I send the minutes to everyone who was there, and I ask them to confirm them. It takes ten minutes, and it saves months.

I coach executives in New York, and many of them are not native speakers of English. When they report a meeting, they use one verb for everything. Said. He said, she said, they said. The problem is that said tells you nothing about the person's attitude. Compare these. She suggested a new date. She insisted on a new date. The first one is an idea. The second one means she won't change her mind. That's a very different message for your boss. Other useful verbs are promised, warned, admitted and agreed. And my last piece of advice. If you're not sure what someone meant, ask them before you report it. A quick question is always cheaper than a big misunderstanding.
